questions.title: GI hormone whose receptor erythromycin activates
questions.question: A 17-year-old man treated with the macrolide antibiotic erythromycin complains of nausea, intestinal cramping and diarrhoea. These effects result from the antibiotic binding receptors on gut enteric nerves and smooth muscle that recognise which gastrointestinal hormone?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrin stimulates acid secretion and mucosal growth; it does not trigger the interdigestive motor pattern that erythromycin mimics.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secretin drives pancreatic bicarbonate secretion in response to duodenal acid and is unrelated to the macrolide effect.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Cholecystokinin causes gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion, not the migrating motor complex activity erythromycin provokes.
explanations.D: Correct. Motilin is the gut peptide that initiates the migrating motor complex during the interdigestive period, exciting smooth muscle directly and through enteric nerves. Erythromycin acts as a motilin-receptor agonist, so it stimulates strong gut contractions. This is why the antibiotic commonly causes nausea, cramping and diarrhoea, and is used clinically as a prokinetic.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Enterogastrone is an inhibitory signal that slows gastric function; it does not mediate the prokinetic action of erythromycin.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 324, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that motilin initiates the migrating motor complex in fasting and that erythromycin is a motilin-receptor agonist.

questions.title: Pancreatic enzyme whose loss causes steatorrhoea in pancreatitis
questions.question: A 67-year-old man with alcohol abuse presents with severe epigastric pain, hypotension, abdominal distension and diarrhoea with steatorrhoea; serum amylase and lipase are raised, confirming pancreatitis. The steatorrhoea is best explained by a fall in the intraluminal concentration of which pancreatic enzyme?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Amylase digests starch; its loss causes carbohydrate maldigestion, not fat in the stool.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Trypsin is a protease; deficiency impairs protein digestion rather than producing steatorrhoea.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Chymotrypsin is also a protease and does not account for fat malabsorption.
explanations.D: Correct. Pancreatic lipase is the major lipolytic enzyme that completes fat digestion in the proximal small intestine. When acinar secretion of lipase falls in pancreatitis, triglycerides are not hydrolysed. The undigested fat then passes into the stool as steatorrhoea, whereas the other enzymes listed act on carbohydrate or protein.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Colipase is only a cofactor that anchors lipase at the lipid interface; the enzyme whose intraluminal concentration primarily determines fat digestion is lipase itself.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 328, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Identify pancreatic lipase as the major lipolytic enzyme whose deficiency causes steatorrhoea.

questions.title: Primary genesis of lower oesophageal sphincter pressure
questions.question: A 53-year-old man with chronic cough and heartburn is found on manometry to have a hypotensive lower oesophageal sphincter with mild reflux. What is the primary genesis of lower oesophageal sphincter pressure in adults?

options.A: Tonic excitatory sympathetic nerve input to the smooth muscle
options.B: Tonic excitatory parasympathetic nerve input to the smooth muscle
options.D: Myogenic properties of the sphincter smooth muscle
options.E: Local production of nitric oxide by enteric nerves

explanations.A: Incorrect. Sympathetic input modulates but does not generate the resting sphincter tone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Excitatory vagal (parasympathetic) input contributes to tone but is not its principal source.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Circulating gastrin has only a minor, non-primary influence on resting sphincter pressure in adults.
explanations.D: Correct. The lower oesophageal sphincter is a high-pressure zone whose resting tone is chiefly an intrinsic (myogenic) property of its circular smooth muscle. Excitatory vagal input and hormones modulate this baseline rather than generate it. When the myogenic tone is lost, gastric contents reflux and cause heartburn.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Nitric oxide from inhibitory enteric nerves relaxes the sphincter; it lowers rather than generates the pressure.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 329, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that resting lower oesophageal sphincter tone is primarily myogenic, with neural and hormonal modulation.

questions.title: Hormone elevated in Zollinger-Ellison acid hypersecretion
questions.question: A 42-year-old man with refractory peptic ulcer disease has data suggestive of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. His raised basal and maximal acid output is best explained by an increase in the plasma concentration of which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Gastrin-releasing peptide is a neurotransmitter that stimulates G cells; it is not the circulating hormone measured to be elevated in this syndrome.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Secretin inhibits acid; indeed it paradoxically raises gastrin in gastrinoma but is not itself the cause of hypersecretion.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Somatostatin inhibits acid secretion, so its increase would lower, not raise, acid output.
explanations.D: Correct. Zollinger-Ellison syndrome is a gastrinoma that secretes large amounts of gastrin outside normal feedback control. The high circulating gastrin drives parietal-cell acid hypersecretion. This produces the characteristic triad of refractory peptic ulceration, raised basal and maximal acid output, and an elevated serum gastrin.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Histamine is the local paracrine amplifier of acid secretion but is not the hormone elevated in the plasma in this syndrome.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 331, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Explain that a gastrinoma (Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) secretes gastrin autonomously, driving acid hypersecretion.

questions.title: Vitamin both made by gut bacteria and absorbed in quantity
questions.question: Which of the following vitamins is both synthesised by intestinal bacteria and absorbed by the host in significant quantities?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Vitamin B6 is obtained from the diet, not from significant host absorption of bacterial product.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Vitamin K is synthesised by intestinal bacteria, but in this bank's framing folic acid is the vitamin taken up by the host in significant quantities; dietary vitamin K intake remains necessary.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Thiamine is a dietary requirement and is not appreciably supplied by gut flora.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Riboflavin must be supplied in the diet and is not significantly derived from bacterial synthesis.
explanations.E: Correct. Several vitamins, including folic acid, vitamin K and some of the B complex, are synthesised by intestinal bacteria. Among the options, folic acid is the one the host absorbs from the intestine in significant quantities. Dietary intake of the others remains necessary because their bacterial product is not efficiently absorbed.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 333, correct = e) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that gut bacteria synthesise folate, vitamin K and some B vitamins, but folic acid is absorbed by the host in significant quantity.

questions.title: Stimulus for gallbladder contraction after a meal
questions.question: A patient's abdominal pain eases after eating. Which statement about gallbladder contraction following a meal is correct?

options.A: It is inhibited by a fat-rich meal
options.B: It is inhibited by the presence of amino acids in the duodenum
options.D: It occurs in response to cholecystokinin
options.E: It occurs simultaneously with contraction of the sphincter of Oddi

explanations.A: Incorrect. A fat-rich meal is the strongest stimulus to gallbladder emptying, not an inhibitor.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Amino acids in the duodenum release cholecystokinin and promote, rather than inhibit, gallbladder contraction.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Vagal cholinergic input aids gallbladder contraction, so atropine blocks it rather than stimulating it.
explanations.D: Correct. Cholecystokinin is released from the upper small intestine by dietary fat and partly digested protein. It contracts gallbladder smooth muscle directly and through a vagovagal reflex, while inhibitory enteric nerves relax the sphincter of Oddi. Together these deliver concentrated bile into the duodenum for fat digestion.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gallbladder contraction is coupled with relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, not its simultaneous contraction, so bile can flow into the duodenum.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 335, correct = d) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: State that cholecystokinin contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi to deliver bile after a meal.

questions.title: Cause of malabsorption in gluten-sensitive enteropathy
questions.question: A 43-year-old woman with bulky diarrhoea, weight loss, microcytic anaemia, low serum calcium and low albumin is diagnosed with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Her generalised fall in intestinal absorption is best attributed to which of the following?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Coeliac malabsorption is not caused by slowed motility; transit changes do not explain the global nutrient loss.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Migrating motor complexes are a fasting motor pattern and are not the mechanism of coeliac malabsorption.
explanations.C: Correct. Gluten-sensitive enteropathy causes autoimmune destruction of intestinal villi, sharply reducing the absorptive surface area. The surviving villous-tip cells also have impaired or absent transporters. As a result absorption of nutrients, minerals, electrolytes and water all fall together, giving the generalised malabsorption seen here.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The enterohepatic circulation is not increased; if anything bile-salt handling suffers, and this does not explain generalised malabsorption.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Gastric emptying is not the limiting step; the defect is in the small-intestinal mucosa itself.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 338, correct = c) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Explain that villous atrophy in coeliac disease reduces the absorptive surface area, causing generalised malabsorption.

questions.title: Mechanism of diarrhoea in lactose intolerance
questions.question: An 18-year-old student has severe bloating and diarrhoea within an hour of dairy products, and her hydrogen breath test is abnormal. The diarrhoea and bloating are best explained by which of the following?

options.A: A deficiency of the brush-border enzyme lactase
options.E: A decrease in exocrine pancreatic secretion

explanations.A: Correct. Lactase, a brush-border enzyme, splits lactose into glucose and galactose. When it is deficient, unabsorbed lactose stays in the lumen and osmotically draws in water, causing diarrhoea. Colonic bacteria then ferment the sugar to gas, producing bloating and the abnormal hydrogen breath test.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The diarrhoea is osmotic, not secretory: it is driven by the unabsorbed sugar's osmotic pull and ceases when lactose is withdrawn.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The absorptive surface is normal; the specific enzyme lactase is lacking rather than the mucosa being reduced.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Only lactose is malabsorbed; general carbohydrate absorption is intact, so this is too broad.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Pancreatic exocrine secretion is normal; lactose is digested at the brush border, not by pancreatic enzymes.

field_notes.keySource: source answer key (PreTest Answers section, item 344, correct = a) with rationale

questions.learning_objective: Explain that lactase deficiency leaves lactose unabsorbed, causing osmotic diarrhoea and bacterial fermentation (bloating).
